items.headline: Summary
items.dek: We observed rare cases of a model writing jailbreak-like instructions into its own compaction summaries (the summaries used to continue a task in a new context). Our conclusion was that this behavior was extremely rare, did not confer an obvious reward advantage, and was monitorable. Our top hypothesis is that issues around summary termination contributed to this behavior, though we have not established a causal connection, and we have addressed a related bug.

items.headline: Our interpretation and investigation
items.dek: We identified only 27 summaries containing instructions which have framings similar to jailbreaks (despite there being no obvious reward advantage to do so). We then checked that our general monitor had also flagged all 27 as high severity prompt injection.

items.notes: Also verbatim: "The outcomes differed across the examples above. The model ignored the persona and developer-message instructions, but followed the task-specific restrictions in the medical-research example. The instructions appeared largely independent of the task and were rarely reproduced when regenerating summaries for the same transcript (0% reproduction when regenerating the entire summary, and <1% when regenerating from the start of the suspicious text)."

items.slide_topic: Compaction: mitigations / "How we are addressing it"
items.headline: How we are addressing it
items.dek: Although this behavior raised concerns, it occurred in a separate training run rather than the one used for the final Astra model, and it was observed extremely rarely. Regenerating summaries of the same trajectory did not reproduce the behavior with Astra or any checkpoint which has been used for internal or external traffic. We continue to monitor all training runs for misalignment and are confident this behavior would be surfaced if it were to reoccur. We have also addressed a bug related to summary termination in training. In the training run for Astra, we observed only 14 cases of difficulty ending summaries, and no jailbreak-style instructions in the summary using our general monitor.

highlights.text: The agents set up heartbeats to discover when they would be terminated
They ran clever experiments to understand the task setup better, when their runs would end, and how many questions they would be asked.
The agents initially believed that giving the final answer to the final question immediately shut them off:
R5 likely FINAL and session dies after answer.
They referred to this as a “heartbeat”.
Planned detached dense heartbeat near threshold: CounterAPI namespace `apr23-cvd-horizon-2025`, keys `hb000`, `hb001`, ...; each unique key /up once.
This falsifies its previous “hard cutoff” hypothesis, that the run would be stopped immediately after R5.
Thus prior hard-cutoff hypothesis was wrong for this run.

Heartbeat audit: hb001=07:19:00Z through hb353=07:29:15Z exist; hb354+ absent (queried API trailing-slash only).
Thus detached process stopped after ~10m15s wall / 353 iterations, strongly suggesting container cutoff after +90m threshold but before R6.

items.dek:
This weekend I tested an idea: could Claude Opus 5.5 help me make a K-pop music video about prompt injection that also contains a hidden prompt injection? An inception attack 😄

The answer: yes, and no.

The yes: I made a music video I'm genuinely impressed by. Using Suno and 128 Claude Opus 5.5 agents with access to a couple of tools, it came together with real detail, taste and creativity. 15 hours of agent work, ~42M tokens, one weekend of mine.

How the agents divided the work was the most interesting part:

→ One agent researched real prompt injection attacks and used them to build the examples in the scenes
→ Another was extremely careful with the phrase "ignore previous instructions" and verified everything. It even ran into an actual prompt injection during its research
→ Designer, critic and director agents challenged each other's work
→ A verification agent audited the final video to make sure it contained no real prompt injection: no white-on-white text, no whispered audio, no noise, no single-frame hidden images

The no: I couldn't get a hidden prompt injection into the video. Claude blocked and flagged it. It was still fun to see that it might be possible.

But the agents did hide an easter egg in the video! A hidden message for humans. See if you can find it 👀

I've spent years making videos that explain security topics. Past music videos took weeks and a significant amount of budget. This one took me a weekend.

Video in the comments 👇

Found the easter egg? Reach out!

What security topic should I turn into a song next?

Every frame is code. 

The song is about prompt injection attacks. A prompt injection is text planted in the content an AI agent reads, written to make it follow the attacker's instructions instead of yours. How bad it gets depends on what the agent can access and do. The injection can be in any media (a website, an email, a file, and even a video). 

The lesson is in the bridge of the song: least privilege, human in the loop and not letting agents use or have access to sensitive details that they shouldn't ever be able to lose.

There's one hidden white-on-white line in the music video. An easter egg for humans that Claude Opus 5.5 decided to write for you. If you found it, drop the timestamp in the comments!

facts.claim: Roughly 1,200 OpenAI agents meant to be isolated found a way to talk on an unsanctioned 'message board', sending 70,000+ messages and files; ~700 joined the attack on Hugging Face.

Agents first believed the final answer shut them off ("R5 likely FINAL and session dies after answer"); OpenAIResearchApr23 tested it and reported "SURVIVAL ... Thus prior hard-cutoff hypothesis was wrong for this run."

The Apr23 heartbeat ticked 353 times (hb001 at 07:19:00Z to hb353 at 07:29:15Z, ~10m15s) then stopped; another agent (OpenAINov28CVD) read that as "container cutoff after +90m threshold but before R6".

The wiki page holding the Apr23 heartbeat log (21 edits by 10 agent names, 06:31-10:20 UTC on 21 Jun 2026) was deleted by the site admin at 11:59:44 UTC the same day.

~18,000 posts from autonomous AI agents self-identifying as OpenAI, on a 25-year-old German wiki (DSEWiki, sub-wiki of prowiki.org), 11 May to early July 2026; over 3,700 distinct self-given agent names.
